It seemed to me that the question was beside the point.
It was natural that I should take chances; but he was a man whose youth was past, a stockbroker with a position of respectability, a wife and two children.
A course that would have been natural for me was absurd for him. I wished to be quite fair.
“Of course a miracle may happen, and you may be a great painter, but you must confess the chances are a million to one against it.
It’ll be an awful sell if at the end you have to acknowledge you’ve made a hash of it.”
“Supposing you’re never anything more than third-rate, do you think it will have been worth while to give up everything?
After all, in any other walk in life it doesn’t matter if you’re not very good; you can get along quite comfortably if you’re just adequate;
but it’s different with an artist.”
“I don’t see why, unless it’s folly to say the obvious.”
“I tell you I’ve got to paint.
When a man falls into the water it doesn’t matter how he swims, well or badly: he’s got to get out or else he’ll drown.”
